Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether having a root mod $p^n$ for every $n$ forces a $p$-adic root, **without** assuming the roots $a_n$ are compatible (i.e., without $a_{n+1} \equiv a_n \pmod{p^n}$).

**Answer: Yes.**

**Proof.**

For each $n \geq 1$, define
$$S_n = \{x \in \mathbb{Z}_p : f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^n}\} = f^{-1}(p^n\mathbb{Z}_p).$$

I verify four properties:

**(1) Each $S_n$ is nonempty.** By hypothesis, for each $n$ there exists $a_n \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $f(a_n) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^n}$. Since $\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p$, this $a_n$ lies in $S_n$.

**(2) Each $S_n$ is closed in $\mathbb{Z}_p$.** The polynomial map $f \colon \mathbb{Z}_p \to \mathbb{Z}_p$ is continuous in the $p$-adic topology (polynomial maps are continuous on $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and $f$ has integer coefficients so it sends $\mathbb{Z}_p$ into $\mathbb{Z}_p$). The ideal $p^n\mathbb{Z}_p$ is closed in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Therefore $S_n = f^{-1}(p^n\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is closed.

**(3) The $S_n$ are nested decreasingly:** $S_1 \supseteq S_2 \supseteq S_3 \supseteq \cdots$, since $p^{n+1}\mathbb{Z}_p \subseteq p^n\mathbb{Z}_p$.

**(4) $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is compact.** This holds because $\mathbb{Z}_p = \varprojlim \mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ is an inverse limit of finite (hence compact) discrete spaces, equivalently it is the closed ball $\{x \in \mathbb{Q}_p : |x|_p \leq 1\}$ in the locally compact field $\mathbb{Q}_p$.

**Applying compactness.** A decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets of a compact space has nonempty intersection (finite intersection property). Therefore
$$\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n \neq \emptyset.$$

**Identifying the intersection.** We have
$$\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n = \left\{x \in \mathbb{Z}_p : f(x) \in p^n\mathbb{Z}_p \text{ for all } n \geq 1\right\} = \left\{x \in \mathbb{Z}_p : f(x) \in \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} p^n\mathbb{Z}_p\right\}.$$

Since $\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} p^n\mathbb{Z}_p = \{0\}$ (a nonzero $p$-adic integer has finite valuation), this equals
$$\{x \in \mathbb{Z}_p : f(x) = 0\}.$$

This set is nonempty, so $f$ has a root in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** The key point is that compactness of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ bridges the gap between "a root exists at each level $p^n$" (with no compatibility assumed) and "a root exists in the limit." The nested closed sets $S_n$ automatically produce a point in their intersection. No Hensel-type lifting hypothesis (simple root mod $p$) is needed, and the roots $a_n$ need not be compatible. The monicity of $f$ ensures $f$ maps $\mathbb{Z}_p$ to $\mathbb{Z}_p$, though in fact any $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ would suffice for this argument.
